items.followUp: Calculate the formula mass of CaCO₃.

rubric.why: The formula contains two K atoms, one S atom, and four O atoms.
rubric.description: Uses the correct atomic masses and counts of atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying the atomic masses and their quantities in K₂SO₄.
Award 1 mark for the final answer, 174 u (or 174 amu).

modelAnswer: Atomic masses: K = 39 u, S = 32 u, O = 16 u.

rubric.why: Iodine-131 is used for medical purposes involving the thyroid gland.
rubric.description: Identifies the thyroid gland as the target.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the thyroid gland or a thyroid disorder.

rubric.why: Iodine-131 is used in the diagnosis and treatment of thyroid disorders, including thyroid cancer.
rubric.description: States a medical use of iodine-131.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is used to diagnose or treat thyroid disorders.

modelAnswer: Iodine-131 is used to diagnose and treat disorders of the thyroid gland, including thyroid cancer.

items.followUp: State the rule used to compare the atomic mass of the middle element in a Dobereiner triad with the other two.

rubric.why: A Dobereiner triad is a group of three elements with similar properties.
rubric.description: Defines the triad as three elements with similar properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is a group of three similar elements.

rubric.why: The atomic mass of the middle element is approximately the arithmetic mean of the other two.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the middle element’s atomic mass is approximately the average of the other two.

modelAnswer: Dobereiner’s triads are groups of three elements having similar properties.
The atomic mass of the middle element is approximately the arithmetic mean of the atomic masses of the other two elements.

items.followUp: Why are the elements of group 13 called p-block elements?

rubric.why: In group 1 and group 2 elements, the differentiating electron enters an s subshell.
rubric.description: Identifies the subshell into which the last electron enters.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the last (or differentiating) electron enters an s subshell.

rubric.why: Their outer electronic configurations are ns¹ for group 1 and ns² for group 2.
rubric.description: Connects the name to the outer electronic configuration of these groups.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving the group 1/group 2 s-subshell configuration or explaining that their outer electrons occupy the s subshell.

modelAnswer: The last (differentiating) electron of group 1 and group 2 elements enters an s subshell.
Their outer electronic configurations are ns¹ and ns², respectively; therefore, they are called s-block elements.

items.followUp: Why does atomic size increase down a group?

rubric.why: Down a group, additional electron shells increase the distance between the nucleus and the valence electrons.
rubric.description: Identifies the increased atomic size or distance down the group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that atomic size, atomic radius, or the distance to the outer shell increases.

rubric.why: Greater distance and shielding weaken the nucleus’s attraction for a shared pair of electrons, so electronegativity decreases.
rubric.description: Explains the reduced attraction for shared electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking increased distance or shielding to weaker attraction and decreased electronegativity.

modelAnswer: Down a group, atomic size and the distance of the valence shell from the nucleus increase.
The attraction of the nucleus for a shared pair of electrons decreases; therefore, electronegativity decreases.

items.followUp: Define a bonding pair and a non-bonding pair of electrons.

rubric.why: A bond pair is shared between two atoms to form a covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a bond pair is an electron pair shared to form a covalent bond.

rubric.why: A lone pair belongs to one atom and is not shared in bond formation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a lone pair is an unshared, non-bonding electron pair.

modelAnswer: A bond pair is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms to form a covalent bond.
A lone pair is a pair of valence electrons that is not shared in forming a bond.

items.followUp: Differentiate between a polar covalent bond and an ionic bond.

rubric.why: In a polar covalent bond, atoms share electrons unequally because their electronegativities differ.
rubric.description: Describes electron sharing in a polar covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electron sharing is unequal in a polar covalent bond.

rubric.why: In a non-polar covalent bond, electrons are shared equally or nearly equally, so poles do not develop.
rubric.description: Contrasts electron sharing in a non-polar covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that sharing is equal (or nearly equal) and the bond has no poles.

modelAnswer: In a polar covalent bond, the bonded atoms share the electron pair unequally, producing partial charges or poles.
In a non-polar covalent bond, the atoms share the electron pair equally or nearly equally, so no poles develop.

items.followUp: What is the Tyndall effect, and in which type of mixture is it observed?

rubric.why: The Tyndall effect is the scattering of light by colloidal particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining the effect as the scattering of light.

rubric.why: The scattered light makes the path of a beam visible in a colloid.
rubric.description: Identifies the particles responsible and the visible beam path.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning colloidal particles and that they make the light beam’s path visible.

modelAnswer: The Tyndall effect is the scattering of light by colloidal particles.
The scattering makes the path of a beam of light visible in a colloid.
